messages.author: 699b1e9dc5d7d443
messages.subject: Is this moderation effect significant?
parts:
Hi Lavaan community,

I ran a moderation model using semTools package and indProd() function.
I used probe2WayMC() and plotProbe() functions to get slopes and plot respectively.

Attached are the results.

My questions are:
1) Is the moderation effect significant in this case?
2) Why the interaction is happening on means?

The sample code run by me is as follows:
library(semTools)
ModerationData <- indProd(Mydata, var1 = c('Item1','Item2','Item3','Item4'),
                          var2 = c('Item5','Item6','Item7','Item8'),
                          match = FALSE, meanC = TRUE, residualC = FALSE, doubleMC = TRUE)

ModerationModel <-
  '
# Independent variable
Indv  =~ Item1 + Item2 + Item3 + Item4 

# Moderting variable
Modv =~ Item5 + Item6 + Item7 + Item8

# Dependent variable
DV1 =~ Item9 + Item10

# Interaction term
IndvXModv =~ Item1.Item5 + Item1.Item6 + Item1.Item7 + Item1.Item8 + Item2.Item5 + Item2.Item6 + Item2.Item7 + Item2.Item8 + Item3.Item5 + Item3.Item6 + Item3.Item7 + Item3.Item8 + Item4.Item5 + Item4.Item6 + Item4.Item7 + Item4.Item8

# Regression
DV1 ~ Indv + Modv + IndvXModv
 '
fit <- sem(ModerationModel, estimator="MLM", data = ModerationData, std.lv = T, meanstructure = T)

#Check means of latent variables
lavInspect(fit, "mean.lv")
# Means of all latent variables came out to be 0 in my case

#Moderation Slope
result2WayMC_DV1 <- probe2WayMC(fit, nameX = c("Indv","Modv","IndvXModv"), nameY = "DV1", modVar = "Modv", valProbe = c(-1,0,1))
result2WayMC_DV1
plotProbe(result2WayMC_DV1, xlim = c(-2,2), xlab = "Indv", ylab = "DV1", legend = TRUE, legendArgs = list())

messages.author: 3fe90052fbf2f899
messages.subject: Re: Is this moderation effect significant?
parts: 1) Is the moderation effect significant in this case?
You can check your summary() output for the effect of the interaction factor (IndvXModv)
2) Why the interaction is happening on means?

I don't understand your question, but the bold comment in your syntax indicates you wonder why your latent means are all zero.  That is the default identification method (freely estimate intercepts of observed variables, fix latent intercepts = 0).  You can see in the help-page examples of probe*() functions how to fix an indicator's intercept for each factor to free its latent intercept, but that is not really necessary.
does interaction always happen at 0 levels of independent and dependent variables using these functions?

It sounds like you are confusing the interaction effect with the simple slopes of the lower-order terms.  Consider reading this primer to make sure you understand what to expect from the output:  http://quantpsy.org/interact/interactions.htm
In such a case how can we conclude a significant interaction effect?

Again, check your summary() output for the effect of the interaction factor (IndvXModv)

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam

messages.author: 82889e926eb5165e
messages.subject: Re: Is this moderation effect significant?
parts:
I think you are stick too much on the terms, like "signifficant", and "there is an intercation effect". These are decisions to be made base on the results.

"Significant" only means that the p-vlaue is lower than an arbitrary value. The p-value for a product term is the change in the focal slope as the moderator increases by 1 unit

I think you are confusing "simple slopes" with "there is an interaction". Even from the plost you attached, you missed to include the simple slopes, but i can see the ones on the right have close slopes as the y axis range is shorter than for the first plot
Simple slopes are the conditional slope of the focal predictor on the outcome, at fixed values of the moderator. This will always change and move, the question is "is the change in slopes large enough for it to be relevant for your constructs"? These will always change because the intercation will almost never be exactly 0. The fact that simple slopes differe doesnt mean that "your intercation is signifficant"

Fro the "signifficant" result from your tables, the slope decreases 0.26 points for each 1 unit that the moderator increases.
For the "non-signifficant" results, the slope increases by 0.073 points for each 1 unit that the moderator increase

Look at the simple slopes, and decide is the change in slope is theoretically meaningful for your research

"Statistically significant" is not a defined "true" in reality, but a simplified decision made from cutoffs criteria

messages.subject: Re: Is this moderation effect significant?
parts:
Harmanjit,

If the slopes are not identical across values of M (moderation is not exactly zero), the lines are definitionally not parallel and will intersect at some value of X. Whether that is at a value of X that is used in your study, or even meaningful, is a  separate question, but it is irrelevant to the identification or statistical testing of an interaction.

The definition of the interaction is that the slopes vary by M. The statistical test of the interaction is whether that variability is detectable in your analysis, most often assessed by p < .05 for the interaction term.. Graphical illustrations are useful supplements to this, but are not the test.

Pat

The SPSS and process macros do the analysis with directly measured variables, these variables have an observed mean, and when included in a regression these are estimated as conditional means (intercepts)

When working with factors, the factors dont have a define mean, the mean is arbitrary in function of the identifications constraints. One of the most common is to fix the mean to 0. You can have an estimated intercept for the factors as long as you fixed other indicator intercepts. But any of these will be arbitrary

On Tuesday, July 20, 2021 at 8:23:14 PM UTC+5:30 mauga...@gmail.com wrote:
I think you are stick too much on the terms, like "signifficant", and "there is an intercation effect". These are decisions to be made base on the results.

"Significant" only means that the p-vlaue is lower than an arbitrary value. The p-value for a product term is the change in the focal slope as the moderator increases by 1 unit

I think you are confusing "simple slopes" with "there is an interaction". Even from the plost you attached, you missed to include the simple slopes, but i can see the ones on the right have close slopes as the y axis range is shorter than for the first plot
Simple slopes are the conditional slope of the focal predictor on the outcome, at fixed values of the moderator. This will always change and move, the question is "is the change in slopes large enough for it to be relevant for your constructs"? These will always change because the intercation will almost never be exactly 0. The fact that simple slopes differe doesnt mean that "your intercation is signifficant"

Fro the "signifficant" result from your tables, the slope decreases 0.26 points for each 1 unit that the moderator increases.
For the "non-signifficant" results, the slope increases by 0.073 points for each 1 unit that the moderator increase

Look at the simple slopes, and decide is the change in slope is theoretically meaningful for your research

"Statistically significant" is not a defined "true" in reality, but a simplified decision made from cutoffs criteria

1) Is the moderation effect significant in this case?

You can check your summary() output for the effect of the interaction factor (IndvXModv)


2) Why the interaction is happening on means?

I don't understand your question, but the bold comment in your syntax indicates you wonder why your latent means are all zero.  That is the default identification method (freely estimate intercepts of observed variables, fix latent intercepts = 0).  You can see in the help-page examples of probe*() functions how to fix an indicator's intercept for each factor to free its latent intercept, but that is not really necessary.


does interaction always happen at 0 levels of independent and dependent variables using these functions?

It sounds like you are confusing the interaction effect with the simple slopes of the lower-order terms.  Consider reading this primer to make sure you understand what to expect from the output:  http://quantpsy.org/interact/interactions.htm


In such a case how can we conclude a significant interaction effect?

Again, check your summary() output for the effect of the interaction factor (IndvXModv)
